HOW_TO_READ_THIS: n = 11 distinct problems, not 80 episodes. Identical tasks give identical outcomes under greedy, so the honest statement is a count of PROBLEMS SOLVED and the percentages are those counts weighted by how often each signature appeared.
the_result: requiring ONE observation before the first hypothesis DOUBLED the problems solved (2 -> 4 of 11) and REDUCED mean actions (10.20 -> 8.82) despite spending a mandatory extra inspect. Cost falls because failures burn the full budget of 12 and successes finish in 3: solving more problems is what makes the average cheaper.
why_it_matters_beyond_G: this is the largest effect found this week in either field, and it is NOT a prior. It is a change to WHEN the agent is allowed to guess. Every experience-prior carrier tested this week -- A, C, F, G-trivial, G-trivial′ -- held capability and failed to reduce cost, or lost capability. Making the agent LOOK BEFORE IT GUESSES did both, and it needed no memory, no vector, no head and no training.
the_compliance_check: all 80 episodes emitted an inspect at step 1 with ZERO forced fallbacks -- the model complied with the instruction rather than being overridden. 11 of 20 episodes in slice 1 hypothesised after one inspect, 9 after two, so the loop constrains the MINIMUM and the agent still chooses to look further.
bounds: n = 11 PROBLEMS. 2 -> 4 is two problems. The 18.8-point gap is those two, weighted.
Not a controlled comparison of the intervention alone: the inspect-first arm sees a different prompt at every subsequent step, so the loop differs throughout, not only at step 1.

This is a HARNESS change. It is not evidence about experience priors; it is evidence about the harness the priors were being measured in, which means every cost number in this line was measured under a loop that guessed before looking.
The prompt gate still REFUSES this loop (7 distinct prompts / 80, ratio 0.0875): more success does not mean more distinguishable state, and no head is fit here.
